facts.text: The Pacific Koel is a brood parasite, laying its eggs in the nests of large honeyeaters such as noisy friarbirds and red wattlebirds.
facts.quote: The Pacific koel is a brood parasite. In Australia, their hosts are mainly large honeyeaters (especially noisy friarbirds and red wattlebirds).

facts.text: Unlike most parasitic cuckoos, Pacific Koel chicks do not try to kill the host's own chicks.
facts.quote: Unlike in other parasitic cuckoos, the young do not attempt to kill the host chicks.

facts.text: The males' repeated calls mark territory and advertise their availability to females at the start of breeding season.
facts.quote: The calls indicate the start of breeding season and males would call repeatedly to mark their territory or communicate their availability to other females.

facts.text: The male Pacific Koel has black plumage often tinted with blue and green, and striking red eyes.
facts.quote: The Pacific Koel can be identified by its black plumage, often tinted with blue and green, and red eyes.

facts.text: The female is brown on the back with white spots and has a cream-coloured underbelly with fine black stripes.
facts.quote: the female has brown plumage along the back with white spots and the underbelly is often cream coloured with fine black stripes

facts.text: In Australia, seeing a Pacific Koel is traditionally taken as a sign that spring and the rainy season have arrived.
facts.quote: In Australia, the presence of the species is regarded as a sign of the arrival of spring and the rainy season.

facts.text: In northern Australia the Pacific Koel is colloquially known as the rainbird or stormbird.
facts.quote: In northern Australia, it is colloquially known as the rainbird or stormbird.

facts.text: Duetting between pairs may hint at short-term pair bonds in this otherwise polygynous bird.
facts.quote: A study of vocalization noted that the duetting behaviour may indicate the possibility of short-term pair-bonding in its otherwise polygynous mating system.

facts.text: The Pacific Koel lives in forest, woodland, plantations and gardens, ranging east to the Solomon Islands and south to eastern Australia.
facts.quote: It is found in forest, woodland, plantations and gardens from Wallacea east to the Solomon Islands and south to northern and eastern Australia.
